Q: How can a class that implements an interface return another interface in a method? A:

s it possible for an object that implements ISorter

Objects don't 'implement _ISorted'. A class might, and an object is an instance of some class. Conflating these notions leads to confusion.

ISorter has a method that returns the interface ISortStats, how does that work?

The concept 'Baker' has a task that returns 'Bread', how is that possible? A baker isn't edible!

The answer should be obvious: The concept of 'maker' is all you need to know. We can abstract the notion of 'food' and we can abstract the notion of 'a thing that makes food'. How do we define this notion? Simple:

interface FoodMaker {
  Food make();
}

So anything that can produce 'food' which is itself an abstract concept can be represented by implementing the interface FoodMaker.

If you're then faced with this situation:

  • I have a bunch of hungry teenagers here! They eat.. well, they will eat pretty much anything. I just need some food! any food!
  • Oh, look, a.. thing that says it can make food.

Grand. You don't need to know more to do the job. Ask the maker of food to make some food and give it to the teenagers. Problem solved. There is no need to ask, or worry about, what kind of foodmaker you've got. There is no point in knowing. Who cares? It's a cook, a microwave with a supply of microwavable meals, or a vending machine. It does not matter. The point of abstraction is that you don't need to know, so that the code can be as generic as possible. We can just do:

void feedHungryTeenagers(List<Teenager> teenagers, FoodMaker maker) {
  for (Teenager teenager : teenagers) {
    Food food = maker.make();
    teenager.feed(food);
  }
}

There is no need to write code to deal with 'well what if the foodmaker is a vending machine?' - we've abstracted all that.

The same thing is happening here. The interface 'ISorter' is the concept of 'a thing that sorts and which can provide statistics about its own sorting process'. And the concept of 'statistics about the sorting process' is itself another interface.

As others have said, this is a pretty bad assignment, and is engaging in some nearly universally derided 'styles'. To wit:

  • Starting interface names with an I is silly. Don't do that.
  • ISortStats as a type name is terrible.
  • ISortStats probably shouldn't be an interface. Why isn't that a concrete class?

Trying to learn what interfaces can do for you by using an example that is not at all suited to interfaces is terrible teaching. Imagine I'm trying to teach you about cooking, and I need to explain how an oven works. I decide to use the oven to store some old shoes.

It can do that, but that's not what it was meant for.

That's presumably the source of all your confusion. The job you've been given can be done, but it doesn't make much sense.
